background.definition: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is descent or herniation of the pelvic organs from their normal position into or beyond the vagina. This descent can include the uterus (uterine prolapse), vaginal apex (apical vaginal prolapse), bladder and anterior wall of the vagina (cystocele), or rectum and posterior wall of the vagina (rectocele). Many women with POP are asymptomatic.

list.listitem: In a follow-up study of 1528 women recruited 5 to 10 years after their first delivery and followed annually for up to 9 years, the 15-year cumulative incidence of POP, based on the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification Examination, was 30.0% (95% confidence interval [CI], 25.1%-34.9%).
Occurs in up to 50% of parous women.

In a cross-sectional study of 1961 nonpregnant women older than 20 years, symptomatic POP was present in 2.9% (2.1%-3.7%) and increased with age, parity, and higher body mass index.This figure of 2.9% (95% CI 2.5-3.4) was confirmed in a more recent study based on data from the National Health and Nutritional Examination Survey.

Racial/ethnic differences were identified by authors of a meta-analysis of 5 population-based US studies with the following pooled prevalence rates: White women: 10.76% (95% CI 10.30%-11.22%), Hispanic women: 6.55% (95% CI 5.83%-7.28%); Black women: 3.80% (95% CI 3.22%-4.38%), and Asian American women: 3.40% (95% CI 2.09%-4.71%). Four of the included studies used questionnaires to determine POP and one used physical examination.

Authors of one study found an increasing rate of seeking medical care for POP based on age - from 1.7/1000 for women aged 30-39 years to 13.2/1000 for women aged 60-69 years and 18.6/1000 for women aged 70-79 years.
Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 studies conducted in low- and middle-income countries found a pooled prevalence of symptomatic POP of 15% (95% CI 10-20%).

Among U.S. women, the lifetime risk of POP surgery is 12.6% to 19.6% (general female population). Authors of an older study of 149,544 women insured through a managed care organization estimated the lifetime risk of a woman undergoing at least one surgery for POP at 6.3%, and the risk of recurrent surgery was 30% by age 80 years.
About 300,000 inpatient procedures are performed annually in the U.S. for prolapse.
Following hysterectomy, prolapse of the vaginal cuff occurs in 6% to 12% of women.
Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is present in 40% to 60% of patients with genital prolapse.

A systematic review identified 60 comparative studies (8 RCTs, 20 cohort studies, and 32 case-control studies; N = 3,567,848 participants) that compared pelvic floor outcomes after hysterectomy vs no hysterectomy. Pelvic organ prolapse was not statistically different within 10 years but was increased after 10+ years (adjusted HR 1.56; 95% CI 1.35 - 1.78). Stress urinary incontinence was increased both within 10 years and after 10+ years (effect size 1.31; 1.06 - 1.56 and ES 2.40; 2.17 - 2.63, respectively).
There does not appear to be a relationship between lifetime physical activity and POP among middle-aged women, although physical activity slightly increases the odds of SUI.

Vaginal apical prolapse commonly accompanies cystocele; in one retrospective study of 385 women, patients with stage 2, 3 and 4 cystocele (see ) had significant apical prolapse (defined as point C of −3 or greater) in 42%, 85% and 100%, respectively.

In one institution’s experience, women with congenital genitourinary anomalies (myelomeningocele, sacral agenesis, bladder exstrophy) presented with POP at a younger age and more advanced stage than women without anomalies.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies including 35,880 patients found a pooled prevalence of occult uterine malignancy at the time of hysterectomy for POP of 0.22% (95% CI 0.11%-0.35%).
Uterine prolapse is caused by weakening of the pelvic connective tissue, pelvic floor ligaments and fascia, and pubococcygeus muscle caused by aging and vaginal birth.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 case-control studies found that the 247 patients with POP had lower expression of collagen type-1 than the 132 patients without POP (odds ratio [OR] 3.23, 95% CI 1.52 to 6.87). Patients with POP also have higher type III collagen gene expression levels than those without POP (standard mean difference 0.32, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.56) based on a meta-analysis of 6 studies.
Loci on several chromosomes may contribute to POP.

In a retrospective analysis of data from women in Washington State, obstetric trauma rates and midforceps rates (1987 through 1999) among women 15-44 years old were strongly correlated with rates of POP surgery among women 25-54 years of age 10 years later (1997 through 2009) (correlation coefficients 0.87 and 0.72, respectively).
In another study from Norway, the odds ratio (OR) of symptomatic POP 15-23 years following operative vaginal delivery was 1.73 (95% CI 1.21-2.48) compared to normal vaginal delivery.
A similar adjusted hazard ratio for operative vaginal delivery compared to spontaneous vaginal delivery of 1.88 (95% CI, 1.28-2.78) was found in a follow-up study of 1528 women.

A systematic review of 60 studies including 8 RCTs concluded that hysterectomy is associated with an increased risk for pelvic organ prolapse after 10+ years (aHR 1.56; 95% CI 1.35 - 1.78). Stress urinary incontinence was increased both within 10 years and after 10+ years. It is also associated with increased risk for stress urinary incontinence, which is modest within 10 years and more than double after 10+ years.

There is controversy about whether higher body mass index (BMI) is a risk factor for POP.Authors of a two-sample Mendelian randomization study based on data from the largest available genome-wide association studies found associations with POP for genetically predicted waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) (OR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01-1.03 per SD-increase) and WHR adjusted for body mass index (OR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01-1.025 per SD-increase).

In one study of women with POP, specific defects identified using static and dynamic MRI were levator muscle weakness (16/34 women), level I and II fascial defects (7/34 women), or both defects (11/34 women).

Oxidative stress has also been posited as a pathogenic factor because sustained mechanical stress, a factor in the appearance of POP, correlates with increased levels of free-radicals production and mitochondrial-induced fibroblasts apoptosis. Oxidative stress hinders normal cellular signaling pathways and interfere with collagen and elastin synthesis.

list.listitem: Although vaginal birth potentially causes weakening of the pelvic ligaments and musculature, data are limited regarding whether cesarean section delivery prevents pelvic organ prolapse (POP). B In a study from Norway, cesarean delivery was associated with a lower risk of symptomatic POP compared to vaginal birth 15-23 years after first delivery with an OR of 0.42 (95% CI 0.21-0.86). In a more recent follow-up study of 1528 women delivered at a community hospital and followed annually for up to 9 years, cesarean delivery was associated with significantly fewer cases of POP (adjusted hazard ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.32-0.67).
Type of directed second-stage pushing (i.e., open or closed glottis) did not influence the occurrence of POP 2 months after delivery based on a secondary analysis of an RCT including 207 women.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies including 696 participants found that bariatric surgery decreased both POP prevalence at 12 months (OR 4.6, 95% CI 2.8-7.6) and symptom severity.

Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) does not appear to be useful during the postpartum period to prevent POP. Among 175 primiparous postpartum women, there was no significant risk difference in POP, bladder neck position, or symptoms of vaginal bulging between women randomized to 4 months of PFMT and control women. B

Similarly, PFMT was not helpful in the perioperative period for women with POP who were undergoing POP surgery for reducing symptoms or improving pelvic floor muscle strength, quality of life or sexual function. B
Intraoperative cystoscopy should be performed to assess possible bladder and ureteral damage after POP or incontinence surgeries; immediate resolution may be possible. C
There does not appear to be a relationship between lifetime physical activity and POP among middle-aged women, although physical activity slightly increases the odds of SUI.

Women with POP present with many physical (e.g., vaginal soreness, vaginal laxity) and sexual complaints (e.g., dyspareunia, sexual avoidance); a vaginal bulge or protrusion is the most useful sign for diagnosis. B
Visual inspection with women supine and standing is used for confirming and staging prolapse and assessing SUI. C
The role of preoperative urodynamic testing (UDT) is unclear. C

list.listitem: Stages of prolapse range from 0 to IV (see ).
Stage of prolapse, however, does not predict symptoms or signs but defines level of bulging/protrusion.

In a study of randomly selected women attending an outpatient clinic of a teaching hospital, although 40% had moderate to large degrees of genital prolapse, symptoms specific to prolapse were only reported on inquiry in about one quarter of them. The most common symptoms were sexual concerns (66.7%) and SUI (60.1%).

In a mailed survey of 141 women in the United Kingdom with symptomatic prolapse and 77 randomly-selected community women, the most common vaginal symptoms that distinguished between the clinic sample and community women were: a "dropping down feeling" (89.9% vs. 6.6%), a lump felt inside (89.3% vs. 2.6%), a "loose vagina" (84.7% vs. 9.2%), a "dragging" pain (82.3% vs. 41.6%), a lump seen outside (75% vs. 1.3%), vaginal soreness (74.5% vs. 42.9%), dry vagina (66.7% vs. 35.5%), painful dryness (62.6% vs. 19.7%), and difficulty inserting tampons (62.9% vs. 2.7%).

In that same survey, the most common distinguishing sexual symptoms were sex life spoilt (85.9% vs. 19%), avoidance of sex (79% vs. 12.5%), worries about sex (79% vs. 14.3%), pain during intercourse (72.6% vs. 30.4%), and relationship affected (67.7% vs. 7.2%).

A 14-item validated self-administered questionnaire may be useful in identifying POP. Items include vaginal symptoms (dragging pain in the lower abdomen, soreness, reduced sensation, laxity or tightness, lump or bulge, dryness, use of vaginally-placed finger to empty bowels, and sexual concerns (vaginal or vaginal symptom interference with sex life). The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines (NICE, 2019) recommend using a validated pelvic floor symptom questionnaire to aid assessment and decision making.

In another study, a patient report of a vaginal bulge had an 81% positive predictive value and a 76% negative predictive value for POP. Urinary splinting was very specific for anterior prolapse, and digital assistance for BMs very specific for posterior prolapse, but neither was sensitive.

Physical examination to detect prolapse is completed with the patient lying and standing. A single (posterior) blade of the speculum can be used to visualize the anterior and posterior vaginal walls, noting the maximal decent in relation to the ischial spines and hymen. Ask the patient to bear down, again noting the maximal decent of prolapse. Repeat with the woman standing and bearing down.

Especially for women with anterior prolapse, stress incontinence can only be adequately assessed by reducing the prolapse (digitally or with a pessary) and having the woman cough; the bladder can be filled retrograde with 300 mL of sterile water or saline to assist detection.

The NICE guidelines (2019) recommend that the physical assessment include the presence and degree of prolapse of the anterior, central and posterior vaginal compartments of the pelvic floor, using the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification system (Table 1), assessing the activity of the pelvic floor muscles and for vaginal atrophy, and ruling out a pelvic mass or other pathology.
A urinalysis is recommended by some authors to check for infection. An ultrasound may be considered if uterine preservation is planned.

In addition to urinalysis, a cough stress test and postvoid residual urine measure is recommended for women with POP by the International Scientific Committee of the Fourth International Consultation on Incontinence. They also suggest imaging of the upper urinary tract (ultrasound or x-ray) for women with severe POP, not being treated.
Cystoscopy should be considered for patients with hematuria, bladder pain, or irritative symptoms despite treatment.

An ultrasound may be considered if uterine preservation is planned. 3D/4D multiplanar and tomographic translabial ultrasound allow visualization of the axial plane and levator ani to assess both avulsion from major maternal birth trauma and hiatal overdistension; both are risk factors for POP and prolapse recurrence.

In one study, translabial three-dimensional ultrasonography demonstrated moderate agreement with MRI in detecting major levator defects (κ = 0.53; 95% CI 0.37-0.69), with a sensitivity of 78% and specificity of 86% (LR+ 56, LR− 025).

The role of preoperative UDT is unclear. Authors of a review article reported that half of women with genital prolapse not reporting symptoms of urinary incontinence (UI) were found to have UI on UDT. In a retrospective study of UDT completed in 43/72 women (60%), investigators found a report of pure SUI in 8 women and detrusor overactivity or mixed incontinence in 13 women. Management was altered in 14 cases (33%) based on the testing including 3 women for whom the surgical procedure was changed.

For patients undergoing invasive urodynamics (e.g., cystometric studies using a bladder catheter), antibiotic prophylaxis does not appear necessary based on consensus, but could be considered for patients with neurogenic bladder or immunosuppression.

Despite information about change in management, it is not clear that additional surgery for UI in patients undergoing POP repair improves outcome (continence). The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guideline disagrees and the authors concluded that for stress-continent women, regardless of preoperative stress testing, the addition of the Burch procedure reduces the risk of postoperative SUI.

Tests to evaluate pelvic floor disorders include dynamic anorectal endosonography, dynamic MRI, and conventional defecography. The American College of Radiology concluded that fluoroscopic cystocolpoproctography and MR defecography are the initial imaging tests of choice for evaluation of POP.

In one study comparing all three tests (performed in 56 women), there were no differences between dynamic anorectal endosonography and dynamic MRI in the number of patients diagnosed with rectocele, perineal descent or enterocele. Patients tolerated the former procedure better and most (72.1%) would choose it over dynamic MRI (25.6%) or conventional defecography (2.3%), if follow-up were necessary.

Women with symptomatic POP present with many physical (e.g., vaginal soreness, vaginal laxity) and sexual concerns (e.g., dyspareunia, sexual avoidance); a vaginal bulge or protrusion is the most useful sign for diagnosis.
Visual inspection with women supine and standing is used for confirming and staging prolapse and assessing SUI.
It is unclear whether preoperative UDT is appropriate or that the potential change in management based on these results improves outcomes.

As many women with POP are asymptomatic, treatment is only indicated if prolapse is causing bothersome bulge and pressure symptoms, sexual dysfunction, lower urinary tract dysfunction, or defecatory dysfunction.

Discuss treatment options including non-surgical management, hysterectomy and surgery that will preserve the uterus, with women who have symptomatic uterine prolapse. NICE provides a patient decision aid that may be helpful for discussing benefits and risks of treatment options.

The 2021 Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SGOC) guideline on apical POP compares different types of surgery with respect to objective and subjective failure rate, reoperation for POP recurrence, complications, and sexual function and can be useful for shared decision-making with patients.

The 2019 ACOG bulletin on POP advises counseling for patients with POP without stress UI undergoing either abdominal or vaginal prolapse repair that postoperative SUI is more likely without a concomitant continence procedure although risk of adverse effects is increased.

Conservative treatment is with pelvic floor muscle exercise and/or vaginal pessaries; supporting data are limited for both. B The use of a pessary results in a clinically meaningful and statistically significant reduction in POP symptoms; however, these findings are limited by the observational nature of the majority of studies and frequent report of adverse effects. Pelvic floor muscle exercise appears to be effective for reducing prolapse symptoms and severity. B

In a systematic review, abdominal sacral colpopexy was better than vaginal sacrospinous colpopexy with respect to recurrence and dyspareunia but was associated with longer operating and recovery time and higher cost. A

Several systematic reviews concluded that mesh or graft inlays improve anatomic results but not functional outcomes and appear to result in worse surgical complications and postoperative adverse events (e.g., new stress incontinence and sexual dysfunction). B The FDA ordered the stopping of sales of transvaginal synthetic mesh products for the repair of POP in 2019. ACOG also suggests that vaginal mesh repair be limited to high-risk women (e.g., those with recurrent POP or medical comorbidities precluding other procedures) after a discussion of risks and benefits.C
The addition of surgery for incontinence in addition to prolapse (Burch colposuspension) improves postoperative continence for many women but increases risk of adverse effects. B
Medications (e.g., adrenergic agents, anticholinergic agents, duloxetine) can be used to improve urinary continence. A

The symptom of stress urinary incontinence may be improved with use of an adrenergic agent (e.g., phenylpropanolamine sustained release 25-100 mg twice daily). Imipramine (10-25 mg daily to 3 times daily) may also be used as well as duloxetine (serotonin-norepinephrine release inhibitor); the former limited by dry mouth and the latter by nausea.
For urge and possibly mixed incontinence, an anticholinergic agent (oxybutynin 2.5-5.0 mg, 3-4 times daily) can be considered.

Topical estrogen may be useful for postmenopausal women for prevention and treatment of vaginal epithelial ulceration. Perioperative vaginal estrogen application does not appear useful for improving surgical success rates after native tissue transvaginal prolapse repair (12-month failure rate of 19% vs. 9% for placebo in one RCT).

NICE (2019) recommends consideration of an estrogen-releasing ring for women with vaginal atrophy and POP who have cognitive or physical impairments that make use of vaginal estrogen pessaries or creams difficult.
In one small RCT, use of dexamethasone 60 minutes prior to vaginal surgery for POP was associated with less nausea/vomiting and need for antiemetics, as well as greater success with voiding trials.

Preoperative pelvic floor muscle injections and pudendal nerve blocks with bupivacaine and dexamethasone did not improve postoperative pain for POP procedures using vaginal native tissue in an RCT with 75 patients.

In an RCT including 119 patients undergoing surgery for POP, a 10-day perioperative course of tamsulosin 0.4 mg beginning 3 days before surgery vs. placebo significantly reduced the risk of postoperative urinary retention (8.8% vs. 25.8%, respectively; OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09-81).

Surgeries for POP can include uterine-sparing surgeries or hysterectomy with uterosacral ligament suspension. Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 studies found no differences between the two for length of hospital stay, recurrence rates, reoperation rates, or voiding dysfunction. Hysteropexy procedures were associated with shorter operative time and fewer visceral injuries. When hysterectomy is performed for POP, ACOG (2019) recommends concurrent vaginal apex suspension to reduce the risk of recurrent POP. Use of mesh (also called vaginal implants) is discussed in a separate subsection below.
Hysteropexy is fixation of the uterus and is an alternative to hysterectomy.

In an RCT, laparoscopic sacrohysteropexy was noninferior to vaginal hysterectomy with suspension of the uterosacral ligaments with respect to apical compartment failure at 12 months in 208 women with POP stage 2 or higher.

At 5-year follow-up of 204 of 208 otherwise healthy women with stage 2 or higher POP who participated in an RCT in the Netherlands comparing sacrospinous hysteropexy with vaginal hysterectomy with uterosacral ligament suspension, there were significantly fewer anatomical recurrences of the apical compartment with bothersome bulge symptoms or repeat surgery in the hysteropexy group (1% vs. 7.8%, respectively). Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs and 5 retrospective studies with 4516 participants, however, found sacrospinous ligament fixation comparable to uterosacral ligament suspension with respect to surgical success, recurrence and total complication rates.

Five-year follow-up of 183 postmenopausal women with symptomatic uterovaginal prolapse enrolled in a multisite RCT comparing sacrospinous hysteropexy with mesh with vaginal hysterectomy with uterosacral ligament suspension identified fewer failures (defined as prolapse retreatment, prolapse beyond the hymen, or prolapse symptoms) for hysteropexy (37% vs 54%, respectively; adjusted hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.36-0.94). With the exception of the Urogenital Distress Inventory, there were no group differences in patient-reported symptoms, general quality of life, or pelvic pain. Adverse events for hysteropexy vs hysterectomy included mesh exposure (8% vs 0%), granulation tissue after 12 weeks (1% vs 12%), and suture exposure after 12 weeks (3% vs 21%).

Authors of a systematic review of 53 studies comparing hysteropexy to POP surgery with hysterectomy, 42 single-arm studies on hysteropexy, and four studies comparing stage ≥2 hysteropexy types found a range of POP recurrence rates from 0% to 29%. Adverse events included mesh exposure (0-39%), urinary retention (0-80%), and sexual dysfunction (0-48%). A laparoscopic approach compared to open surgery was associated with lower recurrent prolapse symptoms (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.07-0.46), urinary retention (OR 0.05, 95% CI 0.003-0.83), and blood loss.

listitem.strong: Uterine, apical, and vaginal vault prolapse

list.listitem: The ACOG 2019 bulletin on POP concludes that uterosacral and sacrospinous ligament suspension for apical POP with native tissue are equally effective treatments.

NICE (2019) guidelines recommend offering women with symptomatic uterine prolapse who have no surgical preference the options of vaginal hysterectomy with or without vaginal sacrospinous fixation with sutures or vaginal sacrospinous hysteropexy with sutures or Manchester repair (excision of the cervix and suture of the cervical stump to the cardinal ligament. Data are limited on comparative effectiveness of various procedures due to largely observational or retrospective cohort studies.

In a non-inferiority RCT including 434 adult patients undergoing a first surgical treatment for uterine descent that did not protrude beyond the hymen, those randomized to the Manchester repair had superior outcomes to the sacrospinous hysteropexy group for a composite outcome of surgical success at 2 years (87.3% vs. 77%, respectively).

In another RCT including 146 patients with symptomatic uterovaginal prolapse, laparoscopic or robotic sacrospinous hysteropexy was non-inferior to vaginal hysterectomy with uterosacral ligament suspension for recurrence of POP at 1-year follow-up (16.4% vs 15.8%, 95% CI -13.0% to 14.2%). The former group experienced longer operating time and early postoperative pain, but there were no differences between groups for length of hospital stay, postoperative complication rates or quality of life and activities of daily living throughout the first postoperative year.

The French National Authority for Health (2021) guidelines recommend laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy for patients with apical and anterior prolapse. Autologous vaginal surgery (including colpocleisis) is recommended as an option for elderly and fragile patients. For cases of isolated rectocele, the posterior vaginal route with autologous tissue is recommended over the transanal route. They state that the decision to place a mesh must be made in consultation with a multidisciplinary team.

Based on a Cochrane review of 40 RCTs of surgery for POP with 3773 women, abdominal sacral colpopexy was better than vaginal sacrospinous colpopexy with respect to recurrence and dyspareunia, but was associated with longer operating and recovery time and higher cost. There was no difference, however, in reoperation rates for prolapse.

The SGOC 2021 guidelines note that while abdominal sacrocolpopexy is superior in some objective outcomes, the procedure is similar to vaginal ligament suspensions for subjective outcomes in the short to medium term and carries a higher risk of mesh exposure over the long term.

For women with vault prolapse, options include vaginal sacrospinous fixation with sutures or sacrocolpopexy with mesh. Women with anterior vaginal wall prolapse should be offered anterior repair without mesh and women with posterior vaginal wall prolapse should be offered posterior vaginal repair without mesh.

In an RCT of 376 participants undergoing apical repair for vaginal vault prolapse, sacrocolpopexy with mesh and transvaginal mesh repair resulted in similar composite failure rates at 36 months and lower failure rates than native tissue repair for the 296 (82%) who completed follow up (28%, 95%CI 20%-37%; 29%, 95%CI 21%-38%; and 43%, 95%CI 35%-53%, respectively); this difference reached significance only when comparing native repair to sacrocolpopexy.

Based on approximately 9-year follow-up of 41 women from an RCT including 74 women randomized to either laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy or abdominal sacrocolpopexy for vaginal vault prolapse, there were no significant differences in quality of life, anatomical results, complications, or reinterventions between groups.

Outcomes and complication rates were similar comparing robotic sacrocolpopexy to laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy for women with uterine prolapse in one RCT, although costs were higher, operating room times longer (202.8 minutes vs. 178.4 minutes), and pain scores 1 week after surgery higher with robotic surgery.

Among women with apical prolapse undergoing transvaginal surgery including midurethral sling, there was no difference between sacrospinous ligament fixation and uterosacral ligament suspension at 2 years with respect to surgical success or serious adverse events. The addition of perioperative pelvic floor muscle training did not improve urinary symptoms at 6 months or prolapse outcomes at 2 years.

In a 5-year follow-up of 244 women (86% of the original participants) who underwent either uterosacral ligament suspension or sacrospinous ligament fixation for vaginal apical prolapse, the two procedures were comparable with respect to surgical failure rate (61.5% vs. 70.3%). Despite surgical failure, defined as apical descent greater than one-third of total vaginal length or anterior or posterior vaginal wall beyond the hymen, retreatment for prolapse or bothersome bulge symptoms, symptom scores remained improved.

Pregnancy outcomes following POP repair were investigated in a systematic review and meta-analysis including 24 studies reporting on 1518 procedures after which 151 patients became pregnant. The Manchester procedure was associated with the highest risk of adverse obstetrical outcomes and preterm premature rupture of membranes. Removing that procedure, sacrohysteropexy was associated with a significantly higher risk of obstetrical adverse outcomes compared to native-tissue procedures.

For anterior repairs, use of mesh or graft inlays reduces the risk of recurrent cystocele but is associated with increased morbidity; for posterior vaginal wall repair versus transanal repair, the vaginal approach reduced the risk of recurrent rectocele. Mesh erosions were reported in 10% of anterior repairs with polypropylene mesh. Finally, there is controversy about whether continence surgery at the time of prolapse surgery reduces the rate of postoperative SUI.

In a review of 5 RCTs and 4 abstracts for cystocele repair, anatomic results were better with mesh but there were no differences in function, including quality of life, between polypropylene mesh and native tissue repairs, with more repeat surgeries due to erosions and other complications with mesh.

In an RCT of 100 women with stage II or greater anterior vaginal wall prolapse, there was no difference at 2-year follow-up with respect to prolapse stage or symptoms between women randomized to anterior colporrhaphy or transvaginal polypropylene mesh insertion. Asymptomatic mesh erosion was seen in 16.4% of the mesh group.

In another RCT of 161 women, however, objective cure rate was significantly higher among women receiving collagen-coated Prolene mesh vs. traditional anterior colporrhaphy (88% vs. 40%, respectively), although there were no other differences between groups with respect to quality of life or symptoms. Vaginal mesh exposure occurred in ten women (13.3%) and dyspareunia in two women in the mesh group at 12 months.

Anterior colporrhaphy with polyglactin 910 mesh and abdominal paravaginal defect repair in one RCT had similar success rates at 2 years, with both groups demonstrating significant improvement in quality of life and similar satisfaction rates (88% and 73%, respectively).
ACOG (2019) recommends transvaginal posterior colporrhaphy over transanal repair for posterior vaginal prolapse.

Authors of a systematic review for rectocele repair also concluded that synthetic mesh was superior to biological materials for anatomical support, but noted that two of three RCTs failed to show a significant difference between synthetic mesh and native tissue repair for posterior vaginal wall prolapse repair.

Laparoscopic sacral colpopexy had a higher satisfaction rate and objective success rate at 2 years than total vaginal mesh (77% vs. 43%, respectively) with lower perioperative morbidity and reoperation rate.

In a secondary analysis of 205 patients undergoing cystocele repair, the prevalence of postoperative pain persisting more than 6 months was 39%. Preoperative pain was the only statistically significant risk factor (OR 2.32, 95% CI 1.24-4.36).

em.strong: Risk factors for de novo stress urinary incontinence (SUI)

list.listitem: Based on two RCTs conducted in the Netherlands of 152 symptomatic women who had at least stage 2 POP and received vaginal prolapse surgery with or without concomitant mid-urethral sling, factors helpful in predicting risk of SUI included age, parity, BMI, use of midurethral sling, urine leakage with urgency, diabetes, and preoperative stress test.
Studies, as shown below, are conflicting on the role of mesh repair on recurrence rates.

In an RCT of 232 women with POP, there was no difference between the mesh repair and biological graft groups. Recurrence was strongly associated with a long-term vegetarian diet (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.12–0.68), long-term soybean product diet (OR 8.01, 95% CI 2.51–25.52), and vaginal intercourse (OR 5.15, 95% CI 1.46–18.18).
ACOG guidelines suggest use of tension-free vaginal tape midurethral sling for women with positive prolapse reduction stress test results undergoing vaginal prolapse repair.
NICE (2019) notes that that there is uncertainty about whether a combined procedure is effective for treating SUI beyond 1 year, and to council women that SUI might persist despite surgery.

In a meta-analysis of seven studies with 1115 women, the risk of postoperative SUI was significantly lower when an incontinence procedure was added to prolapse surgery. However, on pooling these heterogeneous studies and stratifying by preoperative status, the relative risks for women with preoperative SUI were not significantly different with the addition of incontinence surgery while women without preoperative incontinence appeared to benefit (reduced postoperative SUI).

In a later meta-analysis including 10 trials, the reverse was true; authors concluded that women with preoperative SUI symptoms or occult SUI had a lower risk of undergoing subsequent incontinence surgery after vaginal prolapse surgery with a mid-urethral sling than after prolapse surgery alone (0 vs. 40% and 1 vs. 15%, respectively).

In the most recent meta-analysis of 10 studies including 1,361 subjects with POP and stress urinary incontinence, after 6-70 months follow-up the clinical cure rate of those undergoing single TVT or TVT combined with pelvic floor repair was significantly higher than that of patients undergoing other surgeries (OR 3.82, 95% CI 1.39-10.52), with lower clinical complication rates (risk difference -0.09, 95% CI -0.16 to -0.02).

In an RCT of 113 women with SUI undergoing concomitant sacrocolpopexy, those randomized to retropubic midurethral sling vs. Burch retropubic urethropexy reported higher satisfaction (78% vs. 57%) and demonstrated a trend towards higher stress-specific continence rates (74% vs. 57%).

listitem.strong: Mesh use with transvaginal anterior or posterior repair

list.listitem: The ACOG 2019 bulletin on POP concludes that use of mesh for transvaginal repair of posterior vaginal wall prolapse does not improve outcomes. They suggest that vaginal mesh repair be limited to high-risk women (e.g., those with recurrent POP or medical comorbidities precluding other procedures) after a discussion of risks and benefits.
NICE (2019) stated that transvaginal mesh repair of anterior or posterior vaginal wall prolapse should only be used in the context of research due to serious but well-recognized safety concerns.

Cochrane authors found that biological graft repair or absorbable mesh provided minimal advantage compared with native tissue repair. Polypropylene mesh was associated with a reduced risk of recurrence (13% vs. 32%-45%) and surgery for recurrence (2% vs. 2%-7%) but with increased risk of the combined outcome of repeat surgery for SUI, prolapse or mesh exposure (10% vs. 4%-8%). One RCT of vaginal colpopexy repair with mesh versus standard repair was stopped early due to a high vaginal mesh erosion rate of 15.6%.

In 2019, the FDA issued a warning about surgical mesh device complications. In 2021 and 2022, the FDA reported on the final follow-up of patients already enrolled in post-market surveillance studies. They found that Boston Scientific transvaginal POP mesh (no longer commercially available) had similar effectiveness and safety outcomes to native tissue repair at 36 months but continued to believe that devices of this type for transvaginal POP mesh repair presented potential additional risks including mesh exposure and erosion compared to native tissue repair and maintains that these lack a favorable benefit-risk profile. In 2024, the FDA reported their findings on mini-slings finding that clinical performance of stress urinary incontinence mini-slings were comparable to traditional mid-urethral slings; they will continue to consider post-market surveillance studies for mini-slings with novel designs or technological characteristics.

Two parallel UK RCTs were conducted of women undergoing primary transvaginal anterior or posterior compartment prolapse surgery in 35 centers, including 865 in the mesh trial (430 to standard repair alone, 435 to mesh augmentation) and 735 in the graft trial (367 to standard repair alone, 368 to graft augmentation). Augmentation of a vaginal repair with mesh or graft material did not improve women's outcomes in terms of effectiveness, quality of life, adverse effects, or any other short-term outcome, but more than one in ten women had a mesh complication.

Sexual function and de novo and postoperative dyspareunia were similar between the patients who underwent transvaginal mesh repair vs. those who underwent native tissue repair based on a meta-analysis of 17 trials with 2,976 patients.

However, a five-year follow-up of 122 women with severe POP randomly assigned to native tissue repair or synthetic mesh repair found higher cure rate with native tissue when there was prolapse in the posterior and apical compartment but higher for the mesh group in the anterior compartment and in the combination of all compartments. Quality of life was significantly improvement using mesh but complications were significantly higher. Recurrence was higher with repair using native tissue.

While use of mesh in POP surgery may reduce surgical failure rates, complications include higher risks of reoperation for complications (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.2-3.9), vaginal erosion (OR 14, 95% CI 9.1-21.7), vaginal bleeding (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2-2.2), and de novo stress urinary incontinence (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.2-1.8) based on a systematic review of 50 studies.

Authors of a systematic review, meta-analysis, and cost-effectiveness analysis of 27 trials of anterior compartment prolapse involving 8 surgical treatments on 3194 women found synthetic mesh was most effective in preventing recurrence but non-mesh repair had the highest probability of being cost-effective.

In one study, mesh exposure occurred in 30/349 (8.6%); risk factors included smoking before surgery (OR 3.48; 95% CI 1.18-10.28) and having given birth to more than two children (OR 2.64; 95% CI 1.07-6.51).

In an RCT including 46 patients with mild-moderate prolapse, vaginal laser treatment (3-6 applications) was comparable to pelvic floor exercises (9-18 sessions) for symptom improvement measured by the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Distress Inventory at 4 months. At 24 months, 50% (11/22) of laser-patients and 43% (9/21) of PFE-patients requested additional, alternative treatment. High quality evidence with patient-related outcome measures is needed before adopting laser therapy into routine clinical practice.
Interferential current stimulation may also be effective in improving POP stage, pelvic floor muscle strength, and quality of life based on a small sham-controlled RCT.

Obliterative procedures are procedures that narrow, shorten, or completely close the vagina. ACOG suggests consideration of these as first-line treatment for women with significant medical comorbidities who do not desire future vaginal intercourse or vaginal preservation.
Bowel preparation before surgery was without benefit with respect to surgical field and resulted in decreased patient satisfaction and increased abdominal symptoms in one RCT.

Activity restriction following sacrocolpopexy is unnecessary and, in one RCT, the 45 women who liberally resumed their activities reported fewer prolapse and urinary symptoms but similar satisfaction and short-term anatomic outcomes compared to the 50 women in the activity-restriction group.

ACOG (2019) guidelines note PFMT may improve symptoms or slow the progression of POP. NICE (2019) guidelines suggest consideration of supervised PFMT for at least 16 weeks as a first option for women with symptomatic POP.

PFMT provided by a physiotherapist appears to reduce prolapse symptoms and severity; the largest most rigorous trial suggests immediate post-intervention benefit in terms of anatomical and symptom improvement from six months of supervised pelvic floor exercises.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies found that women with symptomatic POP who received PFMT had a greater short-term improvement than controls in prolapse symptom score (mean difference -1.66, 95% CI -2.36 to -0.97).

In the most recent RCT of 414 women randomized to PFMT plus pilates vs. information brochure-only controls, women in the intervention group had improvement of 1.2 points after each follow-up period while control women had no change in symptom scores after the first year and slightly worse scores after 2 years. However, a score improvement of 3 points is needed for a clinically meaningful difference in symptoms and there were no quality-of-life differences at 2 years.

In an RCT of 287 women aged 55 years or over with symptomatic mild prolapse, PFMT vs. watchful waiting did not result in a clinically-important difference in score on the Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory-20, although more women in the intervention group reported overall symptom improvement (57% vs. 13% in the watchful waiting group). Similar score improvement of 12.2 points over 24 months was noted in a primary care RCT with 145 women with symptomatic mild prolapse comparing PFMT with watchful waiting; improved symptoms were reported more often in the PFMT group (43% versus 14% for watchful waiting). A clinically-meaningful change in score was determined to be an improvement of 13.5 points (95% CI 6.2-20.9) in a separate study.
PFMT also reduces urinary incontinence in the short term.

In addition, PFMT may improve sexual functioning. In a small RCT of women with POP, 19 (39%) of women in the PFMT group reported improved sexual function with respect to pelvic floor control, self-confidence, resolution of dyspareunia, and improved libido and orgasms vs. two (5%) in the control group.

PFMT may not be useful postpartum. Among 175 primiparous postpartum women, there was no significant risk difference in POP, bladder neck position, or symptoms of vaginal bulging between women randomized to 4 months of PFMT and control women.

PFMT may not be of benefit following surgery. Among women following vaginal reconstructive surgery for POP, there was no benefit from the addition of PFMT in one small trial. Neither did the addition of PFMT following vaginal apical prolapse surgery improve outcomes at 5-years in one RCT follow-up study.

ACOG (2019), NICE (2019) and SOGC (Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada, 2021) guidelines on POP recommend offering a pessary to women with symptomatic POP as an alternative to surgery. ACOG notes that pessaries can be fitted in most women with prolapse, regardless of prolapse stage.

The use of a pessary resulted in a clinically meaningful and statistically significant reduction in POP symptoms based on a meta-analysis of 6 prospective observational studies and 2 RCTs including 627 participants, most with stage III POP. Findings are limited by the observational nature of the majority of studies and substantial abandonment rates over time. Adverse effects were common and included vaginal discharge (24%), development of urinary incontinence (27%), and vaginal irritation or bleeding (15%). In this study, unsuccessful fitting varied from 15% to 42%.
Long-term follow-up (4 years) of a randomized trial comparing pessary self-management with clinic management found no difference in outcomes. Self-care should be supported.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 primarily cohort studies found higher body mass index, previous reconstructive pelvic surgery (OR 1.705; 95% CI 1.02-2.86), and advanced prolapse (OR 4.2; 95% CI 2.9-6.1) were risk factors for unsuccessful pessary fitting.

Vaginal pessary self-care has similar continuation rates as non-self-care pessary management with pooled continuation rates for self-care of 76% (95%CI 66%-85%, I2=93.3%) based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. Pooled conversion to POP surgery was 12% (95%CI 1-23%).

In the most recent RCT including 440 women with symptomatic stage 2 or greater POP, an initial strategy of pessary therapy, compared with surgery, did not meet criteria for noninferiority with respect to patient-reported improvement at 24 months (76.3% in the pessary group vs. 81.5% in the surgery group). Interpretation is limited by loss to follow-up (20.7% and 26.7%, respectively) and 54.1% participant crossover from pessary therapy to surgery

In an RCT of 276 women with symptomatic POP (stage I-III), use of a pessary plus pelvic floor exercises was more effective than pelvic floor exercises alone with respect to symptom improvement and quality of life.

Types of pessaries include supportive (e.g., ring) or space-filling (doughnut, cube, Gellhorn). A pessary, when fit, should not be visible at the introitus and should not cause pain or pressure for the patient. In one recent randomized cross-over trial (women with a median stage III prolapse), ring and Gellhorn pessaries were equally effective.
Authors of a Cochrane review found a single randomized trial comparing two types of pessaries. Pessaries were helpful in 60% of women and there were no differences between the two types.
In one RCT of 101 women using a vaginal ring pessary for POP, there were no significant differences in satisfaction or complication rates with pessary replacement at 3 or 6 months.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 7 studies found no evidence of deterioration in sexual function and some evidence of improvement for sexually active women using vaginal pessaries for POP.

Estrogen cream can be considered (1-2 times weekly) prior to and during pessary use to ease insertion and reduce risk of some complications. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 3 RCTs, one prospective study and one retrospective cohort study of post-menopausal women with POP using pessaries found use of estrogen reduced the incidence of bacterial vaginosis (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.11-0.72; I2 = 38%) but had no effect on vaginal ulceration, vaginal bleeding or vaginal discharge.

In a secondary-data analysis of 24,928 vaginal procedures, 6834 abdominal procedures, and 1654 obliterative procedures for POP, overall prevalence of composite 30-day major postoperative complications was 3.1%, including 13 perioperative deaths (0.04%), with no difference based on surgical approach.

Urinary tract infection (UTI) is associated with cystocele and constipation/hemorrhoids with rectocele. Pre or postoperative antibiotics do not appear helpful in preventing UTI following midurethral sling with or without concomitant pelvic reconstructive surgery for POP.

Ureteral obstruction was noted in 5.1% of patients following POP surgery in one study; intraoperative cystoscopy was successful in identification of this problem and suture removal relieved obstruction in 88% of cases.

Three cases of small bowel obstruction (SBO) requiring surgery were reported following transvaginal hysterectomy and vaginal vault suspension; the authors suggest that SBO be considered in women with abdominal pain who are post vaginal vault surgery.

Mesh-related complications occur in 5% to 16% of cases, as noted above. In one case series of 347 patients with synthetic mesh-related complications following sling-only procedures for SUI, POP, or sling plus POP, 42.7% had mesh erosion, 34.6% of the patients had pelvic pain, and 30% had dyspareunia. The median number of treatments for mesh complications was 2 (range, 1-9), and 60% required ≥2 interventions (initially surgical for 49% of subjectswith surgery required ford over half[(59.3]) of those managed initially nonsurgicall)y. Translabial ultrasound may be useful for delineating mesh placement and identifying erosion. Authors of a systematic review were unable to find evidence on the most effective management for mesh-related complications.

Recurrent prolapse and/or symptoms of prolapse occur in about a third of women following surgery; incontinence continues/recurs in about 40% (possibly less with use of Burch colposuspension in the short term at 32%). B According to ACOG (2019), reoperation rates are between 6% and 30%, with most estimates at the lower end of the range (19% to 22%).
New pelvic symptoms also occur after reconstructive pelvic surgery; in one study, new symptoms included incontinence (27%) and difficult defecation (22%). B

In one trial of 180 patients (49%) undergoing pelvic reconstructive surgery for prolapse who were working prior to surgery, half returned to work within 35 days after surgery; 13% returned immediately after surgery and 27% returned to work within 2 weeks. C

Successful pregnancies have been reported following uterine-sparing prolapse repairs with both native tissue and mesh-augmented approaches based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies describing 218 pregnancies. POP recurrence occurred in 12% of subjects overall, 15% after vaginal and 10% after abdominal prolapse repairs.

In a longitudinal study of 64 women with symptomatic prolapse who opted for observation as primary management, at a median follow-up of 16 months, only 19% demonstrated progression and most women opted for continued observation. Just over one third (38% [24/64]) requested a pessary trial or surgical correction.
In one case series of 166 women undergoing anterior colporrhaphy, 48% had evidence of cystocele recurrence at a median follow-up of 1.1 years and 27% reported prolapse symptoms.
In a 2-year follow-up study of 306 women undergoing one of two types of native tissue repair for apical prolapse, dyspareunia rates decreased from 25% to 16% but de novo dyspareunia occurred in 10%.

Based on 11 studies reporting some functional outcomes after trocar-guided transobturator vaginal mesh surgery, symptomatic recurrence of POP occurred in between 7% and 33%, de novo SUI in 12% to 17%, persistent urinary incontinence in up to 68%, and dyspareunia worsened or de novo dyspareunia occurred in between 25% and 44%.

In a nation-wide cohort study of 2528 (72%) of 3515 women who had POP surgery in 2015, surgery improved health-related quality of life in 7 of 10 patients over a 2-year follow-up period and patient satisfaction was high (84%).

In a 6-month follow-up study of patients with primary cystocele repair without or with trocar-guided transobturator mesh, sexual function was improved for 53 women in the former group (significant improvement in pain [effect size = 0.5], lubrication [effect size = 0.4], and overall satisfaction [effect size = 0.5] but not in the 54 women in the mesh group. Worsening sexual function was reported in significantly fewer women in the anterior colporrhaphy group compared to women in the mesh group as well (18% vs. 43%). Among 29 men in the study, there was no change in sexual function.

Among 374 women randomized to transvaginal native tissue repair and a midurethral sling with uterosacral or sacrospinous vaginal vault suspension for stages 2-4 apical vaginal prolapse and SUI, pain and functional activity improved below baseline by 4-6 weeks postoperatively and continued to improve for up to 2 years.

In a follow-up study of 103 women (74% of the sample) after a mean of 66 months following laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, 38% continued to have symptoms of prolapse and 32% examined had recurrent prolapse.
In a study from Sweden, at 6 year follow-up from POP surgery, 41% of women reported incontinence episodes, 18% reported vaginal bulging, and 15% refrained from sex because of discomfort or pain.

Using secondary claims data of 49,120 who underwent POP procedures, 40,687 women who underwent SUI+POP procedures and 48,196 women who underwent SUI procedures only, the cumulative incidence of a subsequent SUI or POP surgery within 5 years was 7.8% (95% CI 7.6-8.1) for women younger than 65 years and 9.9% (95% CI 9.4-10.4) for women 65 years or older. The cumulative incidence was higher if an initial POP procedure was performed.
In a long-term follow-up study of 121 women after native tissue repair for stage 2 anterior prolapse, one third required a secondary prolapse compartment procedure from 0.6 to 13 years later.

Among women with symptomatic POP undergoing vaginal surgery in the Vaginal hysterectomy with Native Tissue Vault Suspension vs Sacrospinous Hysteropexy with Graft Suspension Trial, a planned secondary analysis at 5 years revealed that body mass index (increase of 5 kg/m2: adjusted hazard ratio 1.7, 95% CI 1.3-2.2) and duration of prolapse symptoms (increase of 1 year: adjusted hazard ratio 1.1, 95% CI 1.0-1.1) were associated with composite surgical failure, regardless of treatment approach.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 29 studies involving 6597 patients found a recurrence rate of POP after surgery of 37.7%. Significant risk factors for recurrence were levator avulsion (OR 2.46, 95% CI 1.80-3.36), preoperative stage ≥ III (OR 1.87, 95% CI:1.53-2.27), hiatal area on Valsalva maneuver (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.03-1.12) and previous pelvic floor surgery (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.07-2.39). In another meta-analysis of 6 studies examining prolapse recurrence, preoperative prolapse stage (n=5; OR 2.68, 95% CI 1.93-3.73) and age (n=2; OR 3.48, 95% CI 1.99-6.08) were statistically significant risk factors. However, after controlling for stage of prolapse, another study found that older age does not adversely influence the outcomes of POP surgery.
For symptomatic rectocele, a one year follow-up study of 136/160 women (85%) reported persistent symptoms in almost half.

In a follow-up study of 52 women undergoing transvaginal mesh removal, 38% had recurrent or persistent prolapse and 15% underwent a further procedure for prolapse at a mean follow-up of 2.5 years. Fewer women experienced POP recurrence or additional surgery in the same compartment as transvaginal mesh removal (12% and 8%, respectively).
Pessaries can be removed each night, cleaned and replaced in the morning or at least once a week.
Estrogen cream can be considered (1-2 times weekly) prior to and during pessary use to ease insertion and reduce risk of bacterial vaginosis.
Controlling for stage of prolapse, one study found that older age does not adversely influence the outcomes of POP surgery.

feature.caption: International Continence Society Classification System: Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POPQ).
feature.feature_body:
Stage Description
0 No prolapse
I Descent of the most distal prolapse to more than 1 cm above the level of the hymen
II Descent between 1 cm above and 1 cm below the hymen
III Descent more than 1 cm below the hymen but protrudes no further than 2 cm less than the total vaginal length
IV Total or complete vaginal eversion
Data from Bump RC, Mattiasson A, Bo K, et al. The standardization of terminology of female pelvic organ prolapse and pelvic floor dysfunction. Am J Obstet Gynecol 1996;175(1):10–17.
